sections.b: Four explanations have been given for the title shir hamma'alot. (1) Pilgrimage: songs for the journey up to Jerusalem at the feasts (Psalm 122:1–4), the view of most scholars. (2) The temple steps: the Mishnah says fifteen steps led from the Court of the Women to the Court of Israel, "corresponding to the fifteen Songs of Ascents," and that the Levites stood on them with instruments on the Feast of Booths (Mishnah Middot 2:5; Mishnah Sukkah 5:4); the Greek "song of the steps" and Latin canticum graduum reflect this. (3) The return from exile, "the journey up from Babylon" (Ezra 7:9; Psalm 126:1). (4) A stair-step style of verse, in which a word from one line starts the next (Psalm 121:3–8). The views can be combined.
sections.refs: Psalm 120:0; Psalm 122:1–4; Psalm 126:1; Psalm 121:3–8; Ezra 7:9; Mishnah Middot 2:5; Mishnah Sukkah 5:4

sections.h: From Meshech to the night watch
sections.b: The fifteen psalms seem arranged as a journey. Psalm 120 begins far away, "in Meshech" and "among the tents of Kedar"; Psalm 121 lifts its eyes to the hills; Psalm 122 stands "in your gates, Jerusalem"; Psalms 123–131 pass through contempt, danger, tears, toil, persecution, guilt and quiet trust; Psalm 132 brings the ark to its "place of rest"; Psalm 133 gathers the brothers on Zion; Psalm 134 blesses the LORD in his house at night. Psalm 127, the only one linked to Solomon, stands in the middle. The Great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11 (11QPs-a) keeps Psalms 121–132 together but places 133, 134 and 137 elsewhere, so the grouping is that of the Hebrew Psalter, not of every ancient copy. Repeated phrases tie them together: "maker of heaven and earth" (Psalm 121:2; Psalm 124:8; Psalm 134:3), "from this moment on and for all time" (Psalm 121:8; Psalm 125:2; Psalm 131:3) and "Peace on Israel!" (Psalm 125:5; Psalm 128:6).
sections.refs: Psalm 120:5; Psalm 121:1; Psalm 122:2; Psalm 127:1; Psalm 132:8; Psalm 133:1; Psalm 134:1–3

sections.b: Benedict's Rule gives Psalms 120–128 to the short day hours and Psalm 134 to Compline (Rule of Benedict 18). The Roman Liturgy of the Hours uses the Songs of Ascents for Daytime Prayer, and the Orthodox Psalter reads them as the eighteenth kathisma. Medieval monks said all fifteen as the "Gradual Psalms." Many Jewish communities say them on Sabbath afternoons in winter, and the Targum calls each one a song "said on the ascents from the deep," after the legend that David sang them to hold back the waters under the temple (Bavli Sukkah 53a).

common: The Songs of Ascents were sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem for the three feasts.
uncommon: The fifteen songs were sung by the Levites on the fifteen temple steps, one song per step.

claude.title: From Meshech to the seed bag
claude.body: The rare word meshekh appears as the far land of Psalm 120:5 and as the "seed bag" of Psalm 126:6. If the collectors heard the echo, the long exile of the first song becomes the sowing of the seventh, and the return the harvest. This is my suggestion, not a view I have found in the commentaries.

sections.h: Psalm 137: "Happy is the one who grabs your babies"
sections.b: Psalm 137 begins with the exiles weeping "Beside the rivers of Babylon" and ends with the hardest words in the Psalter: "Happy is the one who grabs your babies / and shatters them on the rock" (Psalm 137:9). The speaker asks God to remember Edom's cry on the day Jerusalem fell (Psalm 137:7) and blesses whoever repays Babylon "in full for what you dealt out to us" (Psalm 137:8), the law of like for like (Exodus 21:23–25). The prophets foretold the same for Babylon (Isaiah 13:16; Jeremiah 51:24), and Revelation repeats the demand: "Repay her as she herself has repaid" (Revelation 18:6). Traditions differ. The Roman Liturgy of the Hours leaves out verses 7–9, and the Episcopal Church's 1979 Prayer Book lectionary marks them optional; Jews say the whole psalm before the weekday grace after meals; the Orthodox sing the whole psalm before Lent and read the babies as sins in their infancy; Augustine and Benedict read the rock as Christ; Calvin heard prophecy; Bonhoeffer taught that the curse psalms are prayed through the cross; many modern scholars read them as the honest cry of victims who hand vengeance to God (Romans 12:19).
sections.refs: Psalm 137:7–9; Exodus 21:23–25; Isaiah 13:16; Jeremiah 51:24; Revelation 18:6; Romans 12:19

sections.h: Psalm 129: a curse by withheld blessing
sections.b: Psalm 129 asks that "all who hate Zion" be shamed and become "like grass on a flat roof / that dries out before it can be pulled" (Psalm 129:5–6), so that no one passing will give them the harvest blessing (Psalm 129:8; compare Ruth 2:4). It asks for failure, not death: a milder curse than Psalm 137, but rooted in the same belief that hostility to the city God chose is hostility to God.

sections.h: Psalm 136: loyal love in every verse
sections.b: All 26 verses of Psalm 136 end with the refrain "for his loyal love is forever" (ki le'olam chasdo). The psalm calls every act of God hesed: making the heavens, setting the sun and moon, striking Egypt, dividing the Sea of Reeds, leading through the wilderness, defeating Sihon and Og, giving the land, remembering Israel "when we were brought low," and giving "food to every living thing" (Psalm 136:23–25). The same refrain was sung when the ark came to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:34), at the dedication of Solomon's temple (2 Chronicles 7:3) and at the foundation of the second temple (Ezra 3:11). Psalm 130:7 adds: "loyal love is with the LORD, / and redemption is with him in plenty."

The Talmud calls Psalm 136 the Great Hallel, "because the Holy One, blessed be He, sits in the heights of the world and distributes food to every creature," with Psalm 136:25 in mind (Bavli Pesachim 118a). Opinions there differ on its extent: Psalm 136 alone, from Psalm 135:4, or from Psalm 134. It is said in the Sabbath and festival morning service and at the end of the Passover seder, and the Mishnah has it sung when rain ended a drought (Mishnah Taanit 3:9). The 26 refrains were linked to the 26 generations before the Torah, who lived by God's loyal love alone.

sections.h: Zion in the Songs of Ascents
sections.b: The pilgrim songs speak of Zion as unshakable and blessed. "People who trust the LORD are like Mount Zion: / it will never totter" (Psalm 125:1). God chose Zion as his home: "This is my place of rest forever and ever" (Psalm 132:14). Hermon's dew falls "on the hills of Zion," where "the LORD has ordered the blessing" (Psalm 133:3), and the last song ends, "May the LORD bless you from Zion" (Psalm 134:3; Psalm 128:5). In exile, the singers "remembered Zion" and could not sing "Zion's songs" on foreign soil (Psalm 137:1–4).
sections.refs: Psalm 125:1–2; Psalm 128:5; Psalm 129:5; Psalm 132:13–14; Psalm 133:3; Psalm 134:3; Psalm 137:1–3

sections.b: Psalm 122 is the pilgrim's greeting to the city: "Our feet were standing / in your gates, Jerusalem!" (Psalm 122:2). Built close and joined as one, it is where the tribes go up and David's thrones of justice stand. The prayer plays on its name, Yerushalayim, with shalom, "peace" (Psalm 122:6–8). In exile the singer swears, "If I forget you, Jerusalem, / let my right hand forget" (Psalm 137:5), words Jews still say at weddings, and the Talmud keeps a bare patch of wall in each house in memory of the city (Bavli Bava Batra 60b).
sections.refs: Psalm 122:1–9; Psalm 125:2; Psalm 128:5; Psalm 137:5–7; Bavli Bava Batra 60b

sections.h: The night watch and the ark's rest
sections.b: Psalm 132 recalls David's oath to find "a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob" and the ark's journey to its "place of rest" (Psalm 132:5, 8), lines Chronicles places at the temple's dedication (2 Chronicles 6:41–42). Psalm 134 calls on "all you who serve the LORD, / who stand in the LORD's house night after night" to lift their hands and bless him (Psalm 134:1–2), matching the Levites' night watch (1 Chronicles 9:27, 33). Psalm 135 calls the servants "in the courtyards of our God's house" to praise (Psalm 135:2).

The Songs of Ascents (Psalms 120–134) were probably sung by pilgrims going up for the three feasts. "There the tribes went up, the tribes of Yah, / by a decree given to Israel" (Psalm 122:4) recalls the law of Deuteronomy 16:16. The Mishnah describes Levites on the fifteen temple steps with lyres and trumpets on the Feast of Booths (Mishnah Sukkah 5:4), and the villagers bringing firstfruits up to Jerusalem with flutes (Mishnah Bikkurim 3:2–3). Psalm 134 may be the farewell on the last night of a feast.
sections.refs: Psalm 122:1–4; Psalm 134:1–3; Deuteronomy 16:16; Mishnah Sukkah 5:4; Mishnah Bikkurim 3:2–3

sections.b: Psalm 132 is built on two oaths. David swore not to rest until he found the LORD a dwelling (Psalm 132:2–5); the LORD swore to David, "From the fruit of your body / I will set one on your throne" (Psalm 132:11). Here the promise has a condition: "If your sons keep my covenant ... their sons as well ... will sit on your throne" (Psalm 132:12; compare 1 Kings 2:4), unlike the unconditional promise of 2 Samuel 7:14–16 and Psalm 89:30–37. It closes with a horn springing up and a lamp for God's anointed (Psalm 132:17; 1 Kings 11:36). Peter cites the oath at Pentecost (Acts 2:30).
sections.refs: Psalm 132:1–18; 2 Samuel 7:11–16; Psalm 89:30–37; 1 Kings 2:4; 1 Kings 11:36; Acts 2:30

sections.h: "Up, LORD, to your place of rest"
sections.b: Psalm 132 tells of the ark's search and arrival: "in Ephrathah we heard about it; / in the fields of Jaar we came upon it" (Psalm 132:6), the forest town of Kiriath-jearim where it rested twenty years (1 Samuel 7:1–2). The people bow "at the footstool for his feet" and cry, "Up, LORD, to your place of rest, / you and the ark of your strength!" (Psalm 132:7–8), echoing Moses' cry when the ark set out (Numbers 10:35). Solomon's dedication prayer ends with the same lines (2 Chronicles 6:41), and synagogues sing them when the Torah returns to the ark.

Psalm 137 is the Bible's best-known song of exile: "Beside the rivers of Babylon, / there we sat; we even wept, / as we remembered Zion" (Psalm 137:1). Psalm 126 remembers the return as a dream come true and prays for full restoration, "like the stream beds in the Negev" (Psalm 126:4). Psalm 120 laments living far away, "in Meshech," and Psalm 136:23–24 thanks God "who remembered us when we were brought low." The Al-Yahudu tablets show Judean exiles farming along Babylon's canals in these years.
sections.refs: Psalm 137:1–6; Psalm 126:1–6; Psalm 120:5–7; Psalm 136:23–24; Ezekiel 1:1–3; Jeremiah 29:4–7

sections.b: Psalm 137 sets the exiles "Beside the rivers of Babylon," where their captors demand "Zion's songs" (Psalm 137:1–3), and ends by addressing the city: "Daughter Babylon, you who will be laid waste" (Psalm 137:8). The prophets announced Babylon's fall in the same terms (Isaiah 13; Isaiah 47; Jeremiah 50–51). Babylon fell to Cyrus in 539 BC without being destroyed, and Revelation takes up the psalm's cry against a final Babylon (Revelation 18:6, 21).
sections.refs: Psalm 137:1–9; Isaiah 47:1; Jeremiah 50:15; Jeremiah 51:24; Revelation 18:6; Revelation 18:21

sections.b: Psalm 137:7 asks God to remember "the day of Jerusalem" against Edom, whose people shouted, "Tear it bare! Tear it bare" when Babylon took the city. Obadiah 10–14, Lamentations 4:21–22 and Ezekiel 25:12–14 make the same charge, and 1 Esdras 4:45 says the Edomites burned the temple. The Targum puts the verse in the mouth of Michael, prince of Jerusalem. After AD 70 rabbinic writers read Edom as Rome.

Psalm 130 is the sixth of the church's seven Penitential Psalms (6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143). "If you were to keep watch over guilt, Yah, / Lord, who would remain standing? / Yet forgiveness is found with you" (Psalm 130:3–4). It is prayed in the Catholic Office of the Dead, at every Orthodox Vespers, and by Jews in the Ten Days of Repentance. Luther set it as "Aus tiefer Not" (1524), and Owen wrote a classic exposition of it (1668).

Psalm 130:3 asks who could stand if God kept a record of guilt, and answers, "Yet forgiveness is found with you" (Psalm 130:4). Luther counted it among the "Pauline Psalms" (with Psalms 32, 51 and 143), because it teaches pardon by grace and not by works; Psalm 143:2 and Romans 3:20 make the same point. Catholic tradition prays it as a penitential psalm in which forgiveness also renews the sinner. See the chapter page on Psalm 130 for the traditions.

sections.h: Psalms 127 and 128: house, wife and children
sections.b: "If the LORD does not build a house, / its builders have worked on it for nothing" (Psalm 127:1). Psalm 127 calls children "an inheritance the LORD gives" (Psalm 127:3), and Psalm 128 pictures the wife as "a vine heavy with fruit / deep inside your house" and the children as "young olive plants / set all around your table" (Psalm 128:3). Psalm 128 is a common wedding psalm in Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches. Psalm 127:5, "who has filled his quiver full of them," is cited in Christian debates on family size; see the chapter page on Psalm 127.

Psalm 135:4 praises God because "Yah chose Jacob for himself, / Israel to be his own private treasure," the word segullah of Exodus 19:5 and Deuteronomy 7:6. Psalm 132:13 adds the choice of a place: "Zion is the place the LORD has chosen." 1 Peter 2:9 applies the language of God's treasured people to the church.

Psalm 135:15–18 repeats the mockery of Psalm 115: "The nations' idols are silver and gold, / something human hands have made," with mouths that cannot speak and ears that cannot hear; "not even breath is in their mouths" (Psalm 135:17). Against them stands the LORD who "does" whatever he wants (Psalm 135:6).

sections.h: Sihon and Og in Israel's praise
sections.b: Psalms 135 and 136 both name the two kings east of the Jordan: "Sihon king of the Amorites, / Og king of Bashan" (Psalm 135:11; Psalm 136:19–20). Their defeat was remembered as the first gift of the land, "an inheritance to Israel his people" (Psalm 135:12), and as part of God's loyal love.

Psalm 136 begins its history with creation: God made the heavens "with skill," "stretched the earth flat on top of the waters," and made "the big lights," the sun to govern the day and the moon and stars the night (Psalm 136:5–9; Genesis 1:14–18). Psalm 135:7 adds the storehouses of wind and rain, and the Songs of Ascents call the LORD "maker of heaven and earth" (Psalm 121:2; Psalm 124:8; Psalm 134:3).
sections.refs: Psalm 136:5–9; Psalm 135:6–7; Psalm 121:2; Psalm 124:8; Psalm 134:3; Genesis 1:6–18

sections.b: The Songs of Ascents end with blessings like Aaron's (Numbers 6:24): "May the LORD bless you from Zion" (Psalm 128:5; Psalm 134:3). Psalm 121 is built on the verb "guard, keep" of the same blessing, and Psalm 129:8 shows the harvest greeting "The LORD's blessing on you!" withheld from Zion's enemies.

Psalm 133 compares unity to "good oil on the head / that flows down onto the beard, / Aaron's beard" (Psalm 133:2), the anointing oil poured on Aaron at his ordination (Leviticus 8:12; Exodus 30:22–33). Psalm 132:10 and 132:17 speak of David's "anointed one," the king. Christians read the oil flowing from the head as the Spirit flowing from Christ to the church.

Psalm 127 is the only Song of Ascents linked to Solomon. Its "house" fits the builder of the temple, and its "the one he loves" (yedido, Psalm 127:2) recalls Solomon's birth name Jedidiah, "beloved of the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:25). Chronicles also gives Solomon the lines of Psalm 132:8–10 (2 Chronicles 6:41–42).

In Psalm 137 the exiles "hung up our lyres" on the poplars by Babylon's rivers and refused to sing "the LORD's song / on foreign soil" (Psalm 137:2–4). The psalm's opening has become one of the most set texts in music, from Renaissance motets to Verdi's "Va, pensiero" (1842) and the reggae "Rivers of Babylon" (1970).

Each of Psalms 120–134 is titled "A song of the ascents," except that Psalm 121 has "for the ascents." Four add "Of David" (122, 124, 131, 133) and one "Of Solomon" (127); some Greek copies lack these names. Psalms 135–137 have no title in the Hebrew; the Greek gives Psalm 137 "Of David" and the Gallican Latin "Of David, of Jeremiah." These short titles stand inside verse 1 in Hebrew Bibles, so the verse numbers match English Bibles.
